overview:
In Jain philosophy, the liberated soul—called *siddha*—is a being who has completely and permanently transcended all karmic bondage. Liberation (*moksha*) is not a state granted by divine intervention but the natural condition of the soul once every obscuring, limiting, and deluding karma has been destroyed. A liberated soul exists in its pure, intrinsic qualities: infinite knowledge (*ananta‑jñāna*), infinite perception (*ananta‑darśana*), infinite bliss (*ananta‑sukha*), and infinite energy (*ananta‑vīrya*). These qualities are described across both Digambara and Śvetāmbara traditions, with minor differences in cosmological detail but full agreement on the essential nature of liberation.

Liberated souls reside at the apex of the Jain cosmos, the *siddha-śilā*, a region beyond all movement, change, or rebirth. They do not intervene in worldly affairs, do not create or destroy the universe, and do not maintain relationships with embodied beings. Their existence is characterized by absolute stillness, omniscience, and bliss. Jain texts emphasize that liberation is achieved through the complete annihilation of karmas, which occurs at the final stage of spiritual development, the fourteenth *guṇasthāna*.

The concept of the liberated soul is central to Jain soteriology. It provides the ultimate ethical horizon for lay and monastic practice: nonviolence, truthfulness, non-possession, and disciplined conduct gradually weaken karmic influx (*āsrava*) and support karmic shedding (*nirjarā*). While liberation is considered extremely difficult in the current cosmic era, Jain teachings encourage steady progress toward inner purification, emphasizing that every reduction in karmic bondage brings the soul closer to its natural luminosity.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārtha Sūtra
primary_sources.author: Umāsvāti / Umāsvāmi (accepted by both Digambara and Śvetāmbara traditions)
primary_sources.translation: “Liberated beings possess infinite bliss, infinite memory, infinite knowledge, infinite perception, and infinite energy.”
primary_sources.notes: Tattvārtha Sūtra 10.1 is one of the most authoritative descriptions of the qualities of liberated souls. Commentaries by Pūjyapāda (Digambara) and Siddhasena Gaṇi (Śvetāmbara) affirm that these qualities are intrinsic to the soul once all karmas are destroyed.

primary_sources.title: Samayasāra
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Kundakunda (Digambara)
primary_sources.translation: “The liberated one has reached the end of the world; he is in nirvāṇa and free from all decay.”
primary_sources.notes: Samayasāra emphasizes the pure nature of the soul and describes liberation as the soul’s return to its unconditioned state. The text is foundational for Digambara metaphysics.

primary_sources.title: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra
primary_sources.author: Attributed to early Śvetāmbara canonical compilers
primary_sources.translation: “The liberated possess infinite bliss and infinite perception.”
primary_sources.notes: This canonical text describes the qualities of liberated souls and the path leading to liberation, emphasizing ethical discipline and meditative purity.

misconceptions.myth: Liberated souls act as gods who intervene in human affairs.
misconceptions.reality: Jainism teaches that liberated souls do not influence worldly events. They exist in perfect stillness at the top of the cosmos, free from all activity and relationship.

misconceptions.myth: Liberation means merging with a universal consciousness.
misconceptions.reality: Jain philosophy maintains that each liberated soul retains its individuality forever. There is no merging or dissolution into a collective entity.

misconceptions.myth: Liberation can be granted by divine grace.
misconceptions.reality: Liberation arises solely from the soul’s own effort in eliminating karmic bondage through right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct.
